records.name: Nigeria
records.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

sources.claim: BBC (Aug 2024): Nigerian trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama' found dead - her beaten body was found along an Abuja highway hours after posting about going to see her boyfriend; she had previously expressed fears for her life. Police described her as 'a man fully dressed in female clothing'; same-sex relationships are criminalised in Nigeria and perceived-gay TikTokers face homophobic abuse online.

The Dial (Feb 2025): 'Threats, Raids and Potlucks' - reporting on what it's like to be queer in Nigeria, centred on Abuja Area Mama's killing; six months later no suspects charged; the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation; transphobia and homophobia are common with no legal protections.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026): the UK FCDO's latest Nigeria travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation - same-sex activity illegal with up to 14 years' imprisonment; some northern states operate under Sharia law which can prescribe the death penalty; the SSMPA provides lengthy sentences extending to those who arrange, conduct or attend events perceived as same-sex weddings.

TimesLIVE (March 2025): LGBTQ+ Nigerians recount police abuses under the 'weaponised' law - a 24-year-old man was stopped, beaten and forced to pay a bribe for 'looking gay'; the law creates a climate of hostility making LGBTQ+ people vulnerable to violations by police and the public.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024): 10 years of Nigeria's anti-LGBTQ law - the SSMPA has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, presenting LGBTQI persons as criminals; criminalisation blocks access to redress and justice; job prospects harmed; attacks increased since the law passed.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024): LGBTQ+ Nigerians battle dating-app traps ('kito') - violent entrapment via Grindr and other apps; victims are beaten, filmed, and blackmailed with threats to out them to family; community members fight back with exposure forums and sting operations.

UK Home Office CPIN Nigeria: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics (June 2025, updated April 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Sept 2022) covers transgender Nigerians fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the impact of Nigeria's Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act - the SSMPA's scope is far wider than marriage: it bans cohabitation, 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations (10-14 years); police torture and arbitrary arrests; vigilante groups added homosexuality to their 'terms of reference'.

records.name: Nicaragua
records.summary: Nicaragua demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans (sodomy was decriminalised in 2008), but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGTBIQ+ community in 2024 alone, and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. Since 2018 the Ortega regime has shut down or exiled virtually all independent civil society — including LGBT organisations — so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse; arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents.

sources.claim: F&M Global Barometers country profile for Nicaragua: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Nicaragua: official assessment - no criminalisation but significant societal discrimination; the Ortega government's broader repression affects civil society including LGBT groups.

Amnesty International (May 2019): after a year of protest, Ortega's crackdown continues - at least 325 dead, 2,000+ injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and targeted partly for being gay - the intersection of political repression and homophobia.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua to decriminalise gay sex - the new penal code (effective March 2008) removed the 1992 sodomy law, which had criminalised not only same-sex relationships but was vague enough to permit prosecution of LGBT-rights campaigning or providing sexual-health services.

records.name: Niue
records.summary:
One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust: 'A History of LGBT Criminalisation' - overview of criminalising jurisdictions and strategic litigation (Niue context: no criminalisation as a New Zealand-associated territory).

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

GayLawNet laws page for Niue: age of majority 21 (men)/19 (women) per the Niue Act 1966; age of consent reportedly equalised in 2011; no recognition of same-sex relationships; HIV testing policy for visitors staying longer than two months.

records.name: Netherlands
records.summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Official guidance prepared for WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 confirms there are no visa or entry restrictions based on gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and a 2025 law makes discriminatory motive an aggravating factor that can increase penalties by a third.

The country's institutions are strongly supportive: Amsterdam operates dedicated LGBTQIA+ reporting networks, and the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents in 2026. The capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime.

One caution: reported discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people has risen sharply since 2022 (anti-trans reports rose about 50% in the last year), and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this translates mainly to a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.

sources.claim: WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel page: border/airport procedures, Schengen passport rules, Schiphol logistics, city caution, and a dedicated section for transgender and non-binary visitors; notes the Netherlands ranks #13 on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): progressive laws with gaps - legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter; 'X' marker only via a 3-9 month court procedure; the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation offered to those sterilised under previous rules.

Dutch government page on combating discrimination and violence against LGBTIQ+ people: in 2022 one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation; over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence (17% of trans people, 22% of intersex people); incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence increased sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; lists government measures.

Government.nl overview of new justice and security laws from 1 July 2025 - includes expansion of victims' rights and protection of victim data in criminal case records (general context, not trans-specific).

Equaldex data for the Netherlands: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, discrimination illegal, employment/housing discrimination prohibited on SOGI, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support (52% support LGBT openness; ranked #2 of 121 regions as a 'good place').

NL Times (April 2026): reports of discrimination targeting LGBTQ people jumped 81% since 2022 (4,800 reports last year, +7.5% vs 2024); reports about trans people specifically rose 51% in a year (264 to 399); COC called it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year.

NL Times (July 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of WorldPride in Amsterdam (via the RITA platform) - most from festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA fears the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'; safer spaces set up in hotels, museums and public buildings.

NL Times (June 2026): Amsterdam broadened reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride - 'Safer Spaces' across the city (Nieuwe Kerk, Stedelijk Museum, Stadsarchief, hotels) plus a central RITA location; incidents to be investigated with priority; 1.4 million visitors expected.

NL Times (June 2026): Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride - Mayor Halsema's letter to the council; police/enforcer/organiser agreements to act quickly; recent Prides saw 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports.

OSCE/ODIHR page on the Netherlands' national hate-crime frameworks: Dutch legislation does not include a definition of hate crime; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents.

records.name: Norway
records.summary:
Norway is very safe with strong legal protections and institutional responses, but a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration since 2016; hate speech against trans people is criminalised (2020); anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated Hate Crime Unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

The offsetting factors: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); an anti-gender movement is growing; and underreporting barriers are documented. The security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, but hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction.

sources.claim: Official Norwegian health-rights page on change of legal gender: under the Gender Recognition Act, individuals determine their legal gender based on their own perception of gender identity (self-declaration via the tax office); from age 16 alone, ages 6-16 with parents; under-6s only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers Norwegian citizens resident abroad.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (2020) covers Norway outlawing hate speech against trans people (amendment to the Penal Code).

NRK (May 2024, in Norwegian): big increase in reported hate crime against queer and trans people - record numbers reporting, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% in 2023 and many cases are dropped; many victims have little trust in police; a special hate-crime group encourages reporting.

UiO C-REX blog (Sept 2024) by Christopher R. Fardan: contextualising transphobia in Norway - hostility manifests among political extremists and religious fundamentalists; the Nordic Resistance Movement advocates 'crushing the gay lobby'; research interviews show far-right views of gender diversity as 'degeneracy' and 'paedophilia-normalising'.

UiO C-REX blog (June 2025): why anti-LGBTQI hate crimes are not reported to the police - the HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses found only 8% of victims reported; mistrust in police, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs; those who did report described dismissive or condescending treatment.
OSCE/ODIHR page on Norway's national hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation etc.

Nordisk Post (April 2025): Norway's PST security service reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride; most threat-makers aim to spread fear rather than act.

Life in Norway (updated Nov 2020): 'LGBT Resources in Norway' - Norwegians generally have a liberal attitude; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; gays and lesbians have equal rights in church weddings, adoption and assisted pregnancy; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride, etc.).

records.name: Nepal
records.summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since the landmark 2007 Sunil Babu Pant decision; a third-gender “O” category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled (Rukshana Kapali case) that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu has an established activist scene (Blue Diamond Society, founded 2001).

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: HRW documents (“We Have to Beg So Many People,” 2024) that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces like Madhesh face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside Kathmandu/Pokhara bubbles.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Feb 2024): 'Nepal: Barriers to Transgender Legal Recognition' — despite progressive court rulings, documentary recognition remains bogged in medical and bureaucratic barriers.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali should be legally recognised on all documents as a woman without medical verification - after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021. Context: 'other'/third-gender categories exist since a 2007 ruling, but changing markers to male/female usually requires surgery abroad plus intrusive post-operative genital exams.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's trans-rights reputation needs to be matched with real policy - the country's LGBTIQ+ rights record is more complicated than it first appears; progressive reputation vs implementation gaps.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024): the complexity of transgender life in Janakpur - nine trans people sharing a flat; discrimination in public spaces and government institutions, physical and sexual harassment; celebrated as entertainers but objectified and ridiculed.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: 'The reality of transgender rights in Nepal' - challenges the 'beacon for LGBT rights' narrative; the dominant claim that the Constitution allows self-determined gender markers (from Sunil Babu Pant v Government of Nepal, 2007) masks 'numerous bureaucratic and administrative hurdles and the lack of inclusive legislative measures'; uses the activist-coined term PoMSOGIESC.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.

records.name: Nauru
records.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council; Nauru was among Pacific countries supporting the call.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranking all countries (Germany/Spain top at 4.88; Saudi Arabia bottom at -11.30) - comparative index covering Nauru.

The Guardian (May 2016): Nauru decriminalised homosexuality and attempted suicide - new laws replaced the 1899 Queensland-based criminal code, following a spate of suicide attempts by refugees on the island.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016, but same-sex marriage/unions remain illegal; no explicit legal recognition or protection for intersex and trans people; no employment-discrimination protection; supported the 2011 UN Joint Statement on SOGI; CEDAW Committee categorised as 'No Recognition of LBTI Rights'.

records.name: New Zealand
records.summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit; the Counting Ourselves survey found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats). New Zealand's global-progressive reputation outruns its current street climate.

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.

sources.claim: RNZ (April 2024): reports of hate crimes against trans people jumped 42% (229 incidents in 2023 vs 161 in 2022), spiking 95%+ in the month of Posie Parker's visit; police data likely an undercount as LGBTTQIA+ communities are less likely to report.

RNZ (Feb 2025): the second Counting Ourselves survey (2,631 respondents, 2022) finds almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in four years, 8% experiencing deliberate physical violence; 'alarmingly high' psychological distress and healthcare inequities; researchers call it an emergency.

New Zealand Law Commission Issues Paper 53 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024): a review of the protections in the Human Rights Act 1993 for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics - official law-reform consultation document.

The Spinoff opinion (July 2024) by Jennifer Shields: rainbow communities need protecting and police are failing them - after a spate of rainbow event cancellations; notes wins (BDMSRR Act 2021 for easier ID changes, Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside things getting harder; community safety increasingly on her mind.

Spartacus Gay Travel Index 2026 (Feb 2026): annual index measuring the legal situation and living conditions for queer people in each country across 18 categories (marriage to death penalty); color-coded from dark green (most liberal) to red (most dangerous); explains its rating system including negative points for death-penalty laws and Sharia application.

glbtq encyclopedia entry on New Zealand (Andrew Matzner, 2004): long history of liberal reform (women's suffrage 1893); Gay Liberation Front emerged April 1972; decriminalisation followed years of activism; Georgina Beyer reportedly the first transsexual in the world to achieve national office; 13th country with equal marriage (2013).

PrideNZ.com: over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa New Zealand's LGBTQIA+ rainbow communities, plus a rainbow timeline, 18,000+ GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and the Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates.
